title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm \(A\), and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every supplied integer degree bound \(\Delta\ge2\), and every finite simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), the algorithm produces a proper vertex coloring with colors in \(\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}\) within
\[
C\bigl(\Delta^{1/2-\varepsilon}+\log^*n\bigr)
\]
synchronous communication rounds? The guarantee must hold for every assignment of distinct identifiers from \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\) and every local port numbering. All vertices know \(n\) and \(\Delta\); the same \(\varepsilon,A,C\) must work for all these inputs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm and some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) meeting the stated uniform round bound, or of the logical negation of this existence statement. The improvement may be arbitrarily small but must be one positive constant independent of both \(n\) and \(\Delta\). A negative answer must rule out every positive constant exponent saving in the stated model. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent \(1/2\), or allowing the saving to tend to zero with input size, does not meet the target. There is no prescribed minimum saving and no numerical \(1/100\) answer tolerance for this proposition.
why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
definitions:
The network is exactly the input graph. Graphs may be disconnected and may have isolated vertices, but have no loops, parallel edges, weights or additional structural promises. A supplied \(\Delta\) is any upper bound on all degrees, not necessarily the exact maximum. Proper coloring means that every vertex outputs one allowed color and the two endpoints of each edge output different colors. There is no demand that all colors be used.

Each vertex runs the same finite deterministic program, initially knowing its own identifier, its degree, the local names of its incident ports, and \(n,\Delta\). Port names bijectively number the incident edges at each vertex; names at opposite ends need not agree. The identifier range \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\) fixes the polynomial-ID convention explicitly. Identifiers may be assigned adversarially and may be used arithmetically; no order-invariance restriction is imposed. The initial state contains no global graph description, advice or preprocessing result.

In one synchronous LOCAL round, each vertex sends an arbitrary finite binary message along each incident edge, possibly a different message to each neighbor, and then receives all messages sent to it in that round. Local computation and memory are unbounded, but the program must complete its local steps and eventually output at every vertex. There is no bandwidth restriction, randomness, shared random tape or communication along nonedges. Initially exchanging neighbor identifiers, if needed, costs at most one round and is absorbed by the requested bound. Once all vertices have output, the coloring is final. Elapsed rounds to the last output are counted, rather than total messages, local work or average node time.

The function \(\log^*n\) counts successive base-two logarithms until the value is at most one. The fixed constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen before all graph parameters. It is not an accuracy input; the task does not demand one algorithm for every requested saving. A saving that tends to zero as \(n\) or \(\Delta\) grows is insufficient. Constants hidden in the guarantee cannot depend on graph size, degree bound, port numbering or identifiers.

The target retains only an additive iterated-logarithmic dependence on graph size. A bound polynomial in \(\log n\), even if independent of \(\Delta\), does not establish it in all degree regimes. This is vertex coloring in deterministic LOCAL; results for edge coloring, randomized algorithms, special graph families or massively parallel computation have different guarantees.

progress.text: Theorem 1.3 gives deterministic \(O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)\) rounds for degree-plus-one list coloring, including ordinary coloring as a special case.
The SODA paper records a separate deterministic \(\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)\) bound and improves the Delta-coloring reduction; the degree-exponent target is different.
The updated primary problem list retains the proposed improvement below the square-root degree scale.

context_blocks.text: The source singles out the degree dependence while preserving the smallest standard graph-size overhead. The question is not answered by an improvement that helps only at large degrees relative to graph size.
The list-coloring theorem supplies a square-root degree bound with an additional logarithmic factor under the root; a common palette gives ordinary vertex coloring.
The SODA 2026 work discusses a separate graph-size bound and a reduction for the more restrictive Delta-coloring problem. It does not provide the joint parameter guarantee requested here.

sentences: A proper coloring with \(\Delta+1\) colors always exists for a graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\).
The question asks whether a uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm can find one in \(O(\Delta^{1/2-\varepsilon}+\log^* n)\) rounds for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\).
Any positive constant saving in the degree exponent qualifies, however small, and it must be independent of both graph size and degree.
Processors must reduce a large identifier-based palette without causing conflicts among adjacent vertices acting simultaneously.
Crossing the square-root degree barrier would improve local coordination while preserving the small dependence on total network size.
